[Rod Domowski, 809s]: Catholic Housing Services, or C H S, holds an 8.1 million interim loan for the Aurora Oaks site and shoreline, which was due in June twenty nine, 2026.
[Rod Domowski, 819s]: C H S notified D C H S that it cannot repay the loan or complete permanent supportive housing on schedule due to federal, state, and local funding uncertainties.
[Rod Domowski, 828s]: C H S has proposed a redevelopment plan for one hundred units serving households at fifty to sixty A M I, including partial demolition and new construction.
[Rod Domowski, 837s]: Moving forward on this amended project would require two changes to the interim loan program, which this proposed ordinance would effectuate.
[Rod Domowski, 843s]: First, allowing for an extended loan term of up to an additional five years.
[Rod Domowski, 847s]: And second, raising the permissible area median income from fifty to sixty.
[Rod Domowski, 853s]: As a bit of background, the interim loan program allows for the use of homelessness housing and services program monies, largely document recording fees, and mental illness and drug dependency housing services monies within the housing and community development fund to offer loans to experienced housing developers on a short-term interim basis in order to acquire property for affordable housing and homeless housing.
[Rod Domowski, 873s]: King County Code limits the total loan amount of fifteen million at any given time.
[Rod Domowski, 879s]: King County code also states that the interim loan program is intended to add to the stock of housing for low income and special needs residents.
[Rod Domowski, 886s]: The program is available again to experienced housing developers to acquire property for affordable and homeless housing for households at or below fifty area median income and loans must be repaid within five years.
[Rod Domowski, 898s]: Like I mentioned, King County provided an interim loan of 8.1 million to C H S in June of 2021.
[Rod Domowski, 904s]: It is a five-year loan at three simple interest due upon maturity of the loan, and the loan amount plus interest is estimated at 9.3 million.
[Rod Domowski, 912s]: The project was to acquire a 2.6-acre site and shoreline at the former Oaks at Forest Bay skilled nursing facility to redevelop as permanent supportive housing or an alternate housing strategy.
[Rod Domowski, 924s]: Currently, Lake City Partners Ending Homelessness, or Lake City Partners, operates the sixty-bed Aurora Oaks Enhanced Shelter under an agreement with C H S. Ultimately, C H S intends to redevelop the site as permanent supportive housing, prioritizing those at least twenty five of units for homeless households, and that intent is memorialized in the loan agreement.
[Rod Domowski, 945s]: As the maturity date approached, C H S did notify in early 2025 that it could not fulfill the loan obligations.
[Rod Domowski, 952s]: C H S cited again that federal volatility, particularly with continuum of care homeless housing funding and a limited state and local money to support homeless housing.
[Rod Domowski, 961s]: In the 2026-2027 Biennial Budget Ordinance, Proviso three on the Housing Community Development Fund restricted three hundred,zero until the Executive transmits a report describing the next steps required for the Aurora Oaks Enhanced Shelter to maintain operations as a shelter on site.
[Rod Domowski, 978s]: The Executive transmitted the resulting report on April eight, 2026 with this accompanying proposed ordinance.
[Rod Domowski, 985s]: The report analyzed three options for the continued operations of the enhanced shelter.
[Rod Domowski, 990s]: Option one, to amend King County Code to allow for an extension of C H S's loan, which is recommended by the executive.
[Rod Domowski, 996s]: Option two, foreclose on the C H S interim loan.
[Rod Domowski, 999s]: And option three, purchase the Aurora Oaks site from C H S. The report provides advantages and disadvantages to each, but recommends option one, which would allow the shelter to continue operations onsite until C H S is ready to begin development.
[Rod Domowski, 1015s]: Moving on to the analysis and key issues on page two hundred sixteen of your packet.
[Rod Domowski, 1020s]: Key issue A is the proviso focus.
[Rod Domowski, 1022s]: The intent of proviso P3 was to determine options to allow continued operations of the enhanced shelter in the long term.
[Rod Domowski, 1031s]: The selected option in the report amending the interim loan program focuses primarily on the C H S loan and how to address the fact that the loan was due at the end of June.
[Rod Domowski, 1040s]: While this would allow the Aurora Oaks Enhanced Shelter to continue operations for the time being, it is not a permanent solution as the final C H S project would likely preclude the continued use of the property as a shelter, as interim loan program dollars are required to go towards the development of affordable or homeless housing and not shelters.
[Rod Domowski, 1057s]: Key issue B, project feasibility.
[Rod Domowski, 1060s]: When asked whether the executive believes the project is financially feasible and whether the extended loan would likely result in a completed project, executive staff stated that it is feasible if permitted to do a partial redevelopment of the site.
[Rod Domowski, 1073s]: However, this is dependent on the financial forecast of public funding and relative priorities.
[Rod Domowski, 1077s]: So there is still a risk that extending the loan may not result in a completed project.
[Rod Domowski, 1082s]: Lastly, Key Issue C. If the proposed ordinance is not adopted and C H S is unable to repay the interim loan, the property would technically fall into default and D C H S would need to determine whether to initiate foreclosure proceedings.
[Rod Domowski, 1096s]: Executive staff state that it is likely that D C H S and C H S would seek a remedy in lieu of a foreclosure, which would likely result in King County via the Facilities Management Division becoming owners of the property and C H S foregoing development rights.
[Rod Domowski, 1110s]: There are two amendments included in your packet, which are summarized on page 217.

context_summary:
The July 8th meeting of the King County Council's Budget and Fiscal Management Committee convened with a quorum present, including Chair Rod Domowski, Vice Chair Council Member Barron, and members Rhonda Lewis, Fain, Perry, Mosqueda, and Brown. The minutes from June 10th were approved by unanimous vote (five ayes, zero noes), with Councilmember Mosqueda excused. Public comment was closed due to no attendees signing in or joining online. A consent agenda item for the sale of surplus property at Fauntleroy Way No. 5 was approved and advanced to full council on an expedited basis. The proposed ordinance 20260108 authorizes the sale of 39.1 acres of agricultural land in Townsville District 9, previously held by King County Water and Land Resources Division (Willard), declared surplus on September 8th, 2021, following a F M D surplus declaration analysis. The property was appraised at $600,000 using a sales comparison approach among five land transactions, with the purchase and sale agreement including a reserved agricultural easement; proceeds will support Willard’s acquisition of new open space and recreation facility improvements. Amendment one

The meeting discusses a restrictive covenant requiring agricultural land preservation for thirty years due to conditions set by the State DNR when receiving the property, though no explanation is provided for why it is not perpetual. Council Member Perry raises a question about whether DNR intends to later utilize the property during an interim period and requests offline feedback on this potential use case. A motion is made by Council Member Barone to give a do-pass recommendation to propose Ordinance 20260108, with Amendment One extending the contingency date for council action; the amendment passes unanimously (5 ayes, 0 noes) with Mosqueda excused.
